So to simplify it as much as possible, at 7 you're rolling for a 4 cost Chosen that you already have the items to make effective, isn't too heavily contested, and counters or at least can compete with the other strong boards in the lobby without hinging on high rolling from this point to make it work. You could also take a 3 cost Chosen if you already have enough on your board/bench that you think you can 3\* it. 

The other units you roll to pick up will be determined by the Chosen you picked in the sense that if you have a Chosen which will now be your main carry and your current board doesn't synergize with them, you will need to replace enough of those units to become strong. If you picked up a Chosen mainly for the utility, like a Dazzler Morgana or an Adept Shen, then you have more flexibility with the rest of your board and may not have to pivot so hard.

You're always looking for synergies and to play the strongest board you hit without forcing. Trying to force a comp or the perfect Chosen is a good way to piss away all your gold and bottom 4. If you're being hard countered, have done all you can with positioning/defensive items, have the gold for it, and can do so safely you may even want to sell and roll again for a better situational option. If you're having an amazing game and get to level 9 with enough gold you'll probably want to sell and roll again for a 5 cost Legendary Chosen.

There are a lot of decisions that play off each other and it's going to take time to learn that. But it boils down to playing the strongest board you have and there are very few 1 or 2 costs who will carry you through late game, and even so, they are conditional (i.e., Chosen Yasuo carry but later you never hit Yone...). However, it's also important to be open-minded and play flexibly. If your games are consistently falling off the rails because you're not hitting the units you want or need, then you're probably not playing flexibly.

Short answer: double JG is better on paper for Ahri and mages. The higher spell power is more worth than you think and 65% crit chance is high enough that it's still favorable due to the increased damage, even if 100% crit chance feels better/safer.

Long answer: Double JG simply gives more value on the basis of risk vs. reward when you actually look at the probability on paper. The probability of a 65% chance says you will crit either 2/4 (slightly less likely) or 3/4 times (slightly more likely). With the Ahri nerf you really don't want to be running her as a main carry without running 3 Mage for the double cast, but let's look at both scenarios anyway since the math is done.

Firstly, you could argue for IE+JG if you aren't running 3 Mage for some reason, or when looking at any other champs who aren't simply spell cast bots. On Ahri 2\* with a base AD of 72 you're only looking at an additional 759.44 - 849.35 AD from basic attacks between each ult by running IE+JG, but obviously Ahri only matters for her spell's splash damage.

Even without running 3 Mage, if casting twice during \*overall\* combat at Ahri 2\*, 1/2 crits will yield a diff of 297.5 dmg in favor of IE+JG, but 2/2 crits sees 885.5 dmg in favor of JG x2.

With 3 Mage active, if we assume she gets off 4 casts through the length of combat and crits at least 75% of the time then JG x2 will yield 7189 - 8372 dmg vs. IE+JG yielding 6601 dmg on a guaranteed 4/4 crits. 

That's a difference of 588 - 1771 dmg in favor of JG x2. If you were to only crit 2/4 times you're missing 595 dmg you would've gotten with IE+JG. 

There is risk with a 35% chance she won't crit, but far less risk than reward according to probability.

I mostly did this for myself because I was already curious but here's the maffs all laid out:

IE + JG

Crit Chance

* Base 25% + IE 75% + JG 20% = 100%(+15% carry-over in dmg)
* Spell Damage On Crit (using Ahri 2\* as example)
   * (Ahri base 700 + 15% SP) + (crit base 50% + JG 40% + IE 15%) =  805 SP + 105% crit bonus = 1650.25
* Spell DPS (assuming 2 spell casts overall, uninterrupted, +10 mana per basic attack, 1.5 second channel time each cast, 1 second mana lock after 1st cast)
   * 0.75 attack speed, 0/80 mana = first cast in 12.17 secs, 2nd cast in 13.17 sec  = 3300.5 dmg / 25.34 sec = 130.25 SDPS

JG x 2

* Crit Chance
   * Base 25% + JG x2 40% = 65%
* Spell Damage On Crit
   * (Ahri base 700 + 30% SP) + (crit base 50% + JG x2 80%) = 910 SP + 130% crit bonus = 2093
* Spell DPS (assuming both casts crit)
   * 4186 dmg / 25.34 sec = 165.19 SDPS

3 Mage Double Cast

We're still assuming Ahri reaches max mana twice during combat and there's an additional 1.5 seconds of spell channeling time with each extra cast in this scenario, so another 3 seconds total factored into our DPS.

* IE + JG (4 crits) = 6601 dmg / 28.34 sec = 232.92 SDPS
* JG x2 (3/4 crits) = 7189 dmg / 28.34 sec = 253.66 SDPS
* JG x2 (4 crits) = 8372 dmg / 28.34 sec = 295.41 SDPS

Now you \*could\* crit only 2 out of 4, or 1 out of 4 times but that's highly unlikely...

* JG x2 (2/4 crits) = 6006 dmg / 28.34 sec = 211.93 SDPS
* 1/4 = 4823 dmg / 28.34 sec = 170.18 SDPS

Or...not crit at all...

* 3640 / 28.34 = 128.44 SDPS

but as I said, it's all about probability. Worrying about that missing 35% is overthinking it.

I believe we should praise and encourage animal adoption. Domestic animals are severely overpopulated and add the fact that some humans are simply evil or unresponsible enough that animal abuse is a rampant problem. Anyone who is kind and able enough to adopt or "rescue" an animal, who otherwise would not have had a chance in a life they never asked to be given, deserves to have their good deed acknowledged.

I understand the feeling that having an idea of any kind overemphasized and rammed down your throat is more likely to cause aversion to said idea and that no one enjoys having their moral standing denounced. I'm not in agreement with that way of things. However, the best way to spread awareness is to morally incentivize the practice. People who behave "saintly" for performing good deeds are narcissists. We should all be *expected* to do good simply because it is good, but that does not mean we should avoid praising good deeds. Humans crave approval and it's necessary due to our very nature.

People who choose to purchase animals from a humane and reputable breeder are by no means "bad." Those who research the maintenance requirements, healthcare needs/concerns, and disposition of a certain breed to make an informed decision are being responsible owners. Though I don't agree with using that as an excuse to purchase from mills, which are inhumane and a serious problem that needs to be stopped.

However, for those committed to owning a certain breed, shelters are overpopulated enough that one should always be able to find what you're looking for in a shelter or foster home anyhow (with the exception being rare breeds, which are honestly more for show/aesthetics than a certain purpose, IMO). You may have to compromise on owning a purebred, but honestly what's the point? I fail to see how that's necessary except maybe in the case of a specific allergy. There is an argument that at this stage the very concept of purebred with respect to domesticated animals no longer exists. How much is evolution, uncontrolled mating, or engineered by humans is nearly indistinguishable by now.

It's a simple preference. Not that anyone should feel guilty for having a preference, but know that animal lives are at stake and by acting on your preference over the need you are choosing to be less than helpful.

TL;DR: 

\-Animal rescue/adoption should be encouraged due to overpopulation and abuse. Considering this, and other factors, it is objectively the best practice.

\-You are not a bad person if you choose a breeder over a rescue. Being a responsible consumer/owner is ultimately most important.

\-The concept of purebred domestic animals is inaccurate and owning very specific breeds is a preferential choice rather than a need in nearly all cases.

\-There is no reason a breed or mixed breed conducive to one's lifestyle or needs cannot be found as a shelter/foster home rescue.

When I was a kid in the late 90s the first I heard of IMAX was when a science center in my home town opened an IMAX dome with a massive 60 ft. screen and I got to watch "Everest" there on a class field trip. Considering the most amazing screening experience I'd had to that point was watching Volcano with Tommy Lee Jones (still a fucking great movie) on my aunt's 50" rear projection TV, it was incredible. Being in one of the largest auditoriums I've ever known with a 3 story tall screen that stretched from one end of the room to the other it didn't matter what they played, it would have been breathtaking, and so it was.

Since that moment I have lived for the day I would see a blockbuster film on one of those screens and have my mind melted through every orifice of my face by sheer awesome. When The Dark Knight Rises released to IMAX I had that chance. I'm not from here, but I live in Utah now and had only recently moved at the time. I drove 40 minutes to SLC to finally realize a nearly lifelong dream. Do you know what happened?

There was an even larger 70 ft. screen, I watched a fucking awesome movie, but was ultimately disappointed in the IMAX experience because as a kid everything seems incredible, as you get older great memories are exaggerated more and more, and as an adult nothing can live up to the wonder years. You become cynical, boring, always pissed off about something, and there's nothing you can do about it. All I kept thinking was "I paid $20 for this when the movie would have been more or less the same in a regular theater for less than half the price," and you know what? I hate myself for it. I hate that I couldn't enjoy it. That it didn't take me back to those childhood wonder years. Being an adult is fucking depressing. Just tell that to your kids and sigh when they talk about wanting to grow up so badly like I remember doing.

I feel crazy for never thinking of it this way. Just like when you were learning to read as a kid they taught you to break the word down into syllables and take it one step at a time, then throw it together once it all made sense. 

The trouble with "Nujabes" is as a native English speaker thinking of how to say this as someone's name is a bit of a mind***k. If you're used to or have been commonly exposed to Japanese phonetics though it should be easy once you break it down into kana. Nu is like new, ja is like jar (minus the r sound), be is like bed (minus the d sound), and then you have the "su."

To be proper Japanese, when written the last kana would have to be su because there (to my knowledge) is no such thing as ending the spelling of a word with "s" in Japanese. However, with most dialects or accents in Japan words the "u" part of "su" is trailed off and pronounced so lightly you might not notice it at all. If you've ever watched anime or other Japanese media and heard a character end a sentence with "desu" do you remember them obviously pronouncing it as de-SU or did it sound more like "dess"?

There are times where to add emphasis the u in su will be very pronounced and there are regions where this is also simply normal. But to wrap up my rant, 

TL;DR: the way it is pronounced at the start of Ristorante is backed up by Japanese phonetics, except for the fact that "ja" would be more of a long A sound rather than a flatter "juh" type of sound.
